news.title: An earthquake catches GOP off guard in a county that voted 80% for Trump
news.text:
DARDANELLE — The annual Mount Nebo Chicken Fry, a mainstay of Arkansas politics for generations, saw a break from tradition this year.

In election years, the Democratic and Republican parties usually rent two cabins as their headquarters for the day while they make their case to potential voters lured to the campground by carriage rides, live music and chicken dinners. This year, the Libertarian party rented the Republican cabin.

The problem wasn’t a lack of Republican presence or interest but due to party members having previous commitments, said former Yell County GOP chairman Clay Hooten, who manned a tent the party used instead during the Aug. 29 event.

Even so, the two cabins were surrounded by signs promoting Democratic and Libertarian candidates on the November ballot. Democrat and Libertarian candidates, T-shirts and buttons outnumbered those of Republicans throughout the chicken fry, an unusual sight in the heart of a county where President Donald Trump won nearly 80% of the vote two years ago.

The scene was a small but hopeful sign for Democrats, whose efforts to break Republicans’ lock on Arkansas politics have fallen short for more than a decade. But Trump’s growing unpopularity, a recent poll and national attention surrounding races for the U.S. House and Senate are fueling Democrats’ belief that there’s an opening even in the reddest of states in November.

“I’m tired of people going to the polls to vote against something,” said Kelly Grappe, the Democratic nominee for secretary of state. “I want to give people something to vote for, and I have a vision for this state where the people truly do have a voice.”

The party still faces long odds in Arkansas, where top Republican candidates far outpace their Democratic rivals in fundraising. And at a time when national Democrats and political observers see Senate races in Republican-led states like Texas and Kansas as competitive, Arkansas isn’t viewed the same way. The Cook Political Report classifies the state’s races for governor, U.S. Senate and U.S. House as “solid Republican.”

But, with less than two months before Election Day, Democrats are trying to capitalize on what could be the most favorable political environment they’ve seen in years.

US Senate race heats up

The biggest prize for Democrats would be the Senate seat held by Republican Tom Cotton, the chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee who easily won his second term in 2020 with no Democratic opponent.

He’s seeking a third term against Democrat Hallie Shoffner, a sixth-generation farmer who closed her family’s Jackson County soybean farm last year due to financial strain she attributes to the Trump administration’s tariffs.

An August poll from Talk Business & Politics and Hendrix College showed Shoffner with a slim lead over Cotton, within the margin of error of plus or minus 4.7 percentage points. Shoffner has also made national headlines for her campaign’s focus on her rural background, the increasing cost of living and portraying Cotton’s policy priorities as against Arkansans’ best interests.

Republicans have pushed back on the poll. Another poll from Washington D.C.-based J.L. Partners showed Cotton with a sizable lead over Shoffner, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points.

But the Talk Business poll has ramped up enthusiasm for Shoffner, said Cindy Henry, a retiree from North Little Rock who volunteers for the campaign two days a week.

“We’ll get 40 to 50 calls a day [from] all kinds of people wanting to be heard, with all kinds of issues: personal, medical, jobs, farms, you name it,” Henry said.

Cotton’s campaign emphasizes that he “helped pass the biggest middle-class tax cut in American history, cut regulations to drive down energy production costs, secured the border with President Trump, and fights for a stronger military, bringing home billions of dollars to Arkansas communities in the process,” a spokesperson said in a Friday email.

Two super PACs, America One and Arkansans for Democracy and Justice, have spent more than $3 million combined on text messages and ads assisting Cotton’s bid. His campaign portrays Shoffner as too far left for Arkansas, criticizing her for remarks she made this year supporting defunding Immigration and Customs Enforcement “as it exists right now.”

Cotton’s campaign has also repeatedly highlighted Shoffner’s past donations to 2024 Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris and Democratic U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York.

Shoffner said in an interview that her campaign is “all about Arkansas,” accusing Cotton of trying to find a scapegoat for voters’ frustrations.

“I want to be the kind of public servant that looks to the future, a better future, and moves forward to that future,” she said.

Cotton has consistently allied himself with Trump, whose approval rating in Arkansas and nationwide has declined as the costs of necessities and groceries remain high.

Henry said she’s seen this firsthand as someone on Social Security and managing her family’s farm in Lonoke. Her farming income has plummeted while tariffs have raised the costs of insurance and utilities, she said.

The Arkansans that have contacted Shoffner’s campaign headquarters “want solutions, not rhetoric” and are becoming disillusioned with Cotton’s “same old song and dance,” Henry said.

“We get people that call in that are Republicans that say, ‘I can’t vote for him. Tell me why I should vote for her,’” Henry said.

Libertarian Jeff Wadlin, who is garnering single-digit support in polls, is hoping that voter discontent with both parties could help him.

Wadlin’s candidacy is for “politically homeless” Arkansas voters who “feel like we should just be solving problems like neighbors, working together and not getting angry with each other over cultural issues,” he told the audience at the Mount Nebo Chicken Fry’s pie auction.

Central Arkansas House seat considered in play

All four of Arkansas’ Republican U.S. House members face challengers this year, but it’s the Little Rock area where Democrats are once again directing the most attention.

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee recently added the 2nd District seat held by Rep. French Hill to its list of GOP seats it’s targeting. The Talk Business & Politics poll indicates that Chris Jones, the Democrat challenging Hill in central Arkansas’ 2nd District, has a slim lead over Hill within the margin of error.

This isn’t the first time national Democrats have touted the 2nd District as flippable. Past efforts by Democrats, including by state Sen. Clarke Tucker in 2018 and former state Sen. Joyce Elliott in 2020, have been unsuccessful. And a 2021 redistricting plan that moved some Pulaski County voters into other districts made it more favorable to Republicans.

In an Aug. 19 Fox News appearance, Hill said he’s confident he will win reelection because Arkansans “want to support the most conservative candidate in the race.” He denounced the Democratic Socialists of America in the same segment but did not attempt to tie them to Jones, the Democratic nominee for Arkansas governor in 2022.

But, like Shoffner, Jones has attracted national attention. He won Harris’ endorsement, and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg headlined a rally for Jones.

Jones said the poll numbers and support from outside Arkansas make him “cautiously optimistic and determined.” He says he often reminds voters that Hill’s voting record has aligned with Trump’s priorities, including the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025, which is expected to cut rural Medicaid spending by $15.5 billion per year over the next decade.

“A lot of independents and Republicans are saying, ‘Okay, this is a bridge too far, it’s too much, and it’s time for a new direction,’” Jones said.

Hill said in a Friday email that he’s heard some of the same frustrations from voters: “that the cost of living is out of control, houses are too expensive, filling up the gas tank isn’t affordable, and that Washington doesn’t care about what’s going on.”

He said he’s been “working tirelessly to address” the cost of living, mentioning his support for eliminating taxes on tips and overtime pay.

Hill also sponsored the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a bipartisan bill that became law in July without Trump’s signature, removing some of the regulations on housing manufacturing and bank loans for homebuyers.

Libertarian spoilers?

A major question surrounding Arkansas’ midterm elections is the impact Libertarians could have.

The most prominent of the party’s candidates, gubernatorial hopeful Colt Shelby, had the stage to himself at the Mount Nebo Chicken Fry’s pie auction.

Neither Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders nor her Democratic opponent, state Sen. Fred Love of Mabelvale, was present at the chicken fry.

Shelby is from Franklin County, a typically Republican-voting area frustrated by the Sanders administration’s attempt to build a 3,000-bed prison in the county. He told the Mount Nebo audience that he takes “a common-sense approach” to running for office, which he’s never done before.

“You will not find anybody in this race that will work harder, smarter, better,” Shelby said.

Aaron Bratton, a physician from Russellville, said he’s voting for Shelby because “it’s time for an outsider” who isn’t “politically connected” to be governor because “neither major party represents people anymore.”

Sanders, whose campaign has more than $4.7 million in the bank, hasn’t engaged much with either Shelby or Love. She skipped a gubernatorial debate featuring the two at the Arkansas Press Association’s convention this year. Four years after launching her first campaign with a video prominently featuring Trump, her ads this year so far have focused on state issues like tax cuts and healthcare.

Stele James, who has held leadership roles with the Yell County Democratic Party, said he believes Shelby has a real chance of winning as “that moderate candidate right there on the ground.”

“I see my Republican friends and people on my side that are flocking to his campaign because they’re tired of the divisive nature that the two-party system has produced,” said James, the president of the Two Rivers School District board.

James said he’s also excited about Grappe’s campaign for secretary of state.

Grappe’s GOP opponent is state Sen. Kim Hammer of Benton, who sponsored several 2025 laws placing restrictions on citizens’ ability to change laws and the state constitution via ballot measures. Some of those laws were blocked in federal court on First Amendment grounds last month.

The secretary of state’s duties include oversight of the ballot initiative process, which Grappe said is “absolutely rigged against the people.” She also said she’s met many voters who don’t know what the secretary of state does, and she sees this as a failure of the office’s civic education arm.

Meeting with voters at Mount Nebo, Grappe wore a hat emblazoned with the state’s motto: Regnat populus, Latin for “the people rule.”

Arkansas’ voter turnout has frequently been among the lowest nationwide. This might be due to a shortage of choices that invigorate voters rather than “voter apathy,” said Michael Pakko, chairman of the Libertarian Party of Arkansas and the party’s nominee for secretary of state.

The party is also fielding candidates for lieutenant governor, commissioner of state lands, a handful of state legislative seats and the 1st and 3rd U.S. Congressional Districts.

“I hope that we’ve given you enough choices this year,” Pakko told Mount Nebo attendees.

news.title: N.H. voters choose nominees for open Senate seat, and more races to watch today
news.text: New Hampshire voters are going to the polls on Tuesday to choose Democratic and Republican nominees for retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen's seat, a race that could be key to both parties' efforts to control the upper chamber. Voters in the 1st Congressional District will also be choosing nominees for an open seat, with Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas running for Senate.Here are the races to watch today:New Hampshire Senate raceTo capture the Senate majority, Democrats need to gain four seats and defend every seat they currently control, which includes New Hampshire. While New Hampshire has not voted for a Republican for president since 2000 and has not elected a GOP senator since 2010, Republicans have controlled the governor's mansion since 2017. Former Vice President Kamala Harris won the state by just three points in 2024. Pappas, who has represented the 1st Congressional District since 2019 and is the first openly gay member of Congress from New Hampshire, is facing off in a primary on Tuesday against Karishma Manzur, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America. Shaheen has backed Pappas. There are stark differences between Pappas, a moderate, and Manzur, a medical scientist who has campaigned on progressive policies like Medicare for All and getting money out of politics. Manzur is hoping to pull off an upset similar to Angie Nixon, a Florida state representative and DSA member who won the state's Senate primary in August. Other democratic socialists have won upsets in congressional races in New York and Colorado.Republicans are also choosing their nominee on Tuesday. Former Sen. John Sununu, who was defeated by Shaheen in 2008, is facing off against former Sen. Scott Brown, who represented Massachusetts in the Senate from 2010 until 2013 and lost the Senate race in 2014 against Shaheen. Sununu, who also represented the 1st District from 1997 to 2003, is the brother of popular former Gov. Chris Sununu and the son of former Gov. John Sununu. Sununu, who has Mr. Trump's backing, is the favorite to win on Tuesday. 1st Congressional DistrictThe National Republican Congressional Committee, House Republicans' campaign arm, considers the 1st Congressional District a top target this year. Democrats have held the southeastern New Hampshire seat since 2017, but it was highly competitive in the decade before, switching parties five times since the 2006 election. Nine Democrats are vying for their party's nomination, with a bitter contest having opened up between frontrunners Maura Sullivan and Stefany Shaheen. Sullivan, who served at the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Pentagon during the Obama administration, lost to Pappas in the 2018 Democratic primary. Shaheen, a former Portsmouth city councilor, is the daughter of the current retiring Democratic senator. Sullivan outraised Shaheen by more than $1 million, according to Federal Election Commission data. On the GOP side, five Republicans are competing for the nomination. Mr. Trump gave businessman Anthony DiLorenzo his "complete and total endorsement" in July, calling him "a very successful businessman and entrepreneur." DiLorenzo had a significant fundraising advantage over Novel Iron Works CEO Hollie Noveletsky, who was considered another frontrunner, but the most recent polling showed the two were statistically tied in the race. New Hampshire governor's raceRepublican Kelly Ayotte, first elected in 2024, is running for a second term. She faces two primary challengers on Tuesday, but she is expected to easily win the nomination. Democrat Cindie Warmington is running unopposed for the party's nomination.
news.summary: Both Democrats and Republicans are targeting the Senate seat that will be vacated by Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, who is not running for reelection.

news.title: Becerra once pushed for the death penalty, but says he would extend a moratorium if elected governor
news.text: Democrat Xavier Becerra defended the death penalty while serving as California's attorney general, a punishment his office actively sought in the case of a gunman convicted of an Orange County mass shooting, but as the front-running candidate for governor he has vowed to block executions if elected in November. Becerra said he will extend the blanket reprieve for all death row inmates that Gov. Gavin Newsom enacted by executive order in 2019, saying he supported "moving our state away from a costly, flawed system that disproportionately impacts Black and brown communities and too often gets it wrong." Those comments have reassured anti-death penalty advocates wary of Becerra, who has stated throughout his career that capital punishment should be an option for victims seeking justice. He reiterated that stance just a decade ago during his confirmation hearing for attorney general, though he also expressed concerns about the unjust application of the punishment. “I support the death penalty, but I hate the way it’s being executed,” Becerra told state lawmakers in 2017. “If you commit some heinous crime where you have taken the life of someone else, and you knew that there was a death penalty in place in that place where you committed that crime, then you should face the punishment for what you've done,” he explained. “It doesn't give me pleasure to say that, but I simply do believe there's a simple justice in that.” Becerra's challenger in the Nov. 3 election, former Fox News commentator Steve Hilton, opposes the death penalty but said he would rescind Newsom's moratorium because it defies the will of voters. Becerra has said he is concerned by how death sentences historically have been applied, including a highly disproportionate number of condemned inmates who are Black or Latino men and cases in which they later have been exonerated of crimes. He repeated similar positions last year during a gubernatorial forum in Los Angeles. “I do not believe every Californian has gotten a fair verdict in these fights,” he said in response to a question about extending Newsom’s moratorium. “But here is what I will tell you: We have to be aggressive in going after crime, especially the most heinous crime. … I will make sure that we have a judiciary system and a prosecution system that takes into account that we must show fairness.” Though California has not performed an execution since 2006, prosecutors in some areas of the state continue to seek and win death sentences. As of early August, there were 565 condemned inmates in California prisons, according to the state Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation. Newsom's moratorium stops the state from carrying out those sentences. In California, county district attorneys are responsible for prosecuting the vast majority of accused murderers when they go to trial and also deciding whether to seek the death penalty. The office of the state attorney general is responsible for defending death penalty convictions on appeal. Becerra sought the death penalty in a murder case his office prosecuted early in his tenure, though unsuccessfully. Scott Dekraai, who was convicted of killing his ex-wife and seven others in a shooting at a Seal Beach beauty salon, was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole after a prosecution scandal involving his case. Some death penalty opponents criticized Becerra for fighting to uphold the death sentence of Robert Lewis Jr., who was deemed by the California Supreme Court in 2018 to have an intellectual disability that made him ineligible for execution. “I find that reprehensible,” said Mike Farrell, president of Death Penalty Focus, an advocacy group. A longtime anti-death penalty activist, Farrell is better-known for starring as B.J. Hunnicutt in the TV show "M*A*S*H." “It may not have been his idea, but he was part of that process," he said of Becerra. Others said Becerra cannot be blamed for doing his job. Former Vice President Kamala Harris faced the same dilemma when she served as state attorney general, as does Rob Bonta, who currently holds the office. “The AG is in a different position because it's just inherent in their role to defend convictions and sentences,” said Natasha Minsker of the California Anti-Death Penalty Coalition. “For example, Kamala Harris is very strongly personally opposed to the death penalty and still, while she was AG, the office defended hundreds of death sentences. Same with Rob Bonta. He's very clearly personally against the death penalty, and his office continues to defend death sentences.” Becerra’s campaign declined an interview on the subject and referred to his statement in support of extending Newsom’s freeze on executions. Hilton, his Republican opponent in the race, holds starkly different views. “If you're arguing that taking a life is such a serious crime, then I don't think responding by taking a life actually makes that argument,” he said in an interview last month. But he said California voters spoke clearly by voting twice — in 2012 and 2016 — against ballot measures that would have repealed the death penalty. “I don’t think it’s OK for a governor to just substitute their personal opinion on an issue where the voters had an explicit and direct say,” he said. “I strongly believe in holding people accountable for what they do,” Hilton said. “But my sort of fundamental belief is that if we're saying it's wrong to kill someone, then the state shouldn't be doing it, either." Hilton also would roll back Democratic-led reforms that have shortened many inmates' prison sentences by allowing them to seek parole sooner. Even if a governor rescinds the moratorium, resuming executions would be a long and complicated process because the state has no approved protocol or facilities to carry out death sentences. Newsom ordered the dismantling of San Quentin’s death row and execution chamber. Even before he took office, the state’s use of lethal injection drugs was part of a long-running and now-dormant legal battle. And a dwindling number of attorneys who specialize in death penalty cases meant 70% of condemned inmates did not have a lawyer at the end of last year, according to a state report. California’s death penalty also faces a new legal challenge from groups arguing that capital punishment cases have been administered in a way that is racially discriminatory. In May, the California Supreme Court ordered the attorney general’s office to respond to the arguments and assigned the case to a superior court. The shifts in California’s criminal justice system are reflected in legal battles waged by the pro-death penalty Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, a nonprofit that supports victims of crime and their families in court. “We used to do a lot of work in the capital punishment area because that was the area where justice and the sentences were under the greatest attack,” said Kent Scheidegger, the group’s legal director. But as California’s Democratic-controlled Legislature, governor and, at times, voters adopted measures aimed at reducing the prison population, Scheidegger said the foundation's efforts increasingly are focused on preserving “the finality of sentences.” Many capital cases were negotiated as “plea bargains to life without parole on the express promise that this will provide the finality that the victims need most,” he said. “Life without possibility of parole, until recently, meant life without possibility of parole. And now we've got one action after another coming out of the government to break down that finality and give people sentenced to life without parole opportunities to get out.” The group has challenged attempts to expand early release for violent offenders under 2016’s Proposition 57 and new regulations that would allow people sentenced to life without the possibility of parole to seek release. Twenty-seven states allow the death penalty, but governors in four of them — California, Ohio, Oregon and Pennsylvania — have paused executions. Attitudes about capital punishment have shifted over time. A 2025 Gallup poll showed 52% of Americans favor the death penalty for people convicted of murder, down from its peak of 80% in 1994. In a 2023 survey by the Public Policy Institute of California, 62% of adults in the state said they “strongly favor” or “somewhat favor” the death penalty in murder cases. When asked which punishment they prefer for a first-degree murder case, 55% said life without parole and 43% chose the death penalty. More than three-quarters believe there “is some risk that an innocent person will be put to death.” Despite the changing opinions, Minsker, of the California Anti-Death Penalty Coalition, said there’s little appetite for another repeal attempt because of how expensive ballot measure campaigns have become. “I am personally one of the strongest proponents of ending the death penalty, and I am not sure I would spend $30 million on that right now, given all the other needs that California has,” said Minsker, a former attorney for the American Civil Liberties Union who ran the unsuccessful 2012 death penalty repeal measure. Putting an anti-death penalty measure on the statewide ballot also could have put Newsom in an precarious political position. If it failed, Californians would be sending a stinging rebuke to the Democratic governor's executive decision to grant a blanket reprieve to all condemned inmates. Minsker is leading a group of criminal justice advocates, faith organizations, prosecutors, murder victim family members and others urging Newsom to commute every death sentence in California before he leaves office. But advocates are unsure whether Newsom, who is considering a run for president in 2028, would risk the backlash a mass commutation would probably bring. The California Supreme Court also must review executive clemency actions for inmates with more than one felony charge. Commuting all death sentences to life in prison “would be the coup de grâce,” Farrell said. “However, politically, I'm sure those who are advising him are urging him to have caution in that regard.”
news.summary: California's next governor will decide whether to continue a moratorium on executions. Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton hold very different views on the death penalty.

news.title: Why the road to House and Senate majorities runs through New Hampshire
news.text:
New Hampshire is one of the final states to hold its primaries this year, and there is no doubt that the road to a successful midterms will be paved in the Granite State.

While more and more states have become more uniformly Republican or Democratic, in New Hampshire, split-ticket voting remains common, even routine, despite Republican control of the governor’s office, Executive Council and both chambers of the state Legislature. Yet Democrats hold both Senate seats and both House seats. In a state where diversity of ideas and thought is still reflected at the ballot box, candidates and campaigns matter more, and voters can shake hands and speak directly with those running multiple times throughout the campaign.

With senior Sen. Jeanne Shaheen retiring, the open Senate seat is a must-hold for Democrats to flip the chamber as a whole, and a big opportunity for Republicans.

Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas is now running for the Senate. He is a four-term congressman who has won in a GOP-leaning district, including beating Karoline Leavitt in a general election in 2022. But in order to make it to the general, he must prevail in Tuesday’s primary against a relatively unknown progressive challenger, scientist Dr. Karishma Manzur. Polls show Pappas with a lead but a recent University of New Hampshire poll showed his margin shrinking. Add in the unpredictability of primaries this year, and this contest is worth watching closely, at least as a test of Pappas’ strength ahead of a competitive general election.

On the Republican side are two former senators who have both lost races against Shaheen. Scott Brown, who represented Massachusetts in the Senate, moved north after losing to Elizabeth Warren in 2012, and ran unsuccessfully against Shaheen in 2014. His opponent, John E. Sununu, is looking to regain the seat he lost in 2008. In addition to his term in the Senate and three terms in the House, Sununu is part of the state’s political royalty: His brother just finished eight years as a popular governor, and his father served as governor and White House chief of staff to George H.W. Bush.

Thanks to his name and a Trump endorsement, Sununu is almost assured a primary win. But the president’s backing could be problematic in a general election, since Trump’s approval ratings in New Hampshire are negative by 20 points or more. Recent polls of a Sununu-Pappas matchup show a close race, ranging from a 7-point Pappas advantage to a 2-point Sununu lead.

The race to replace Pappas in the state’s first congressional district is heating up, too. The Democratic field of eight candidates includes Shaheen’s daughter Stefany Shaheen, former Obama administration official and Marine veteran Maura Sullivan, and union activist and teacher Carleigh Beriont. The race has been somewhat ugly with accusations of AIPAC influence, nepotism and which candidates are authentic progressives. Polls show Sullivan with a narrow lead over Shaheen, but with many voters undecided and a large field, anything could happen.

In the Republican primary, the two major candidates are Trump-backed developer Anthony DiLorenzo and metal fabrication business owner Hollie Noveletsky, who finished second in the 2024 GOP primary. Recent surveys show nearly half of voters undecided.

Two years ago, Pappas carried this district by roughly 8%, and Kamala Harris carried it by just 2%. Whoever emerges from Tuesday’s contests, Democrats simply have to win this district if they hope to win a House majority.

Finally, New Hampshire’s outsize influence on presidential nominations makes it attractive for ambitious out-of-state politicians. Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., will be at the Democrats’ Labor Day Breakfast, as will progressive California Rep. Ro Khanna. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg will attend a fundraising dinner for the state party. Other potential Democratic candidates have already made stops in the state, including Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and California Gov. Gavin Newsom. Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., will visit the state the day after the primary and his fellow Republican Rick Scott will be there the following week for a dinner.

New Hampshire may be the ultimate skeleton key to GOP or Democrat majorities. But it is also clear that some are eager to help their party’s fortunes now in order to increase their own fortunes in the future. Election Day this year is Nov. 3. The presidential race in New Hampshire begins Nov. 4.

news.title: Trump Has Brutalized Blue States in His Second Term. There’s a Way for Democrats to Fight Back.
news.text:
This is the second in a series of articles, “Try, Try Again?,” drawn from my new book—Great and Dangerous Offences: The Case For (and Against) Impeaching Trump a Third Time—due out in early 2027.

The Constitution created a federal republic consisting of states with equal legal status. Under the 10th Amendment, Congress and the executive branch have only limited authority to intrude on the sovereign prerogatives of the states. Individual residents of those states are guaranteed equal protection of the laws. These are pillars of the American constitutional order. To subvert any of them is to subvert the Constitution itself, a subversion that, as the Framers insisted, is impeachable.

If a president engages in a pattern of conduct that subordinates the rights and interests of individual states to his personal or partisan political interests, that would be impeachable. Likewise, if a president engages in a pattern of conduct that denies equal protection of the laws of the United States to the citizens of individual states in order to promote his personal or partisan political interests, that, too, would be impeachable. In his second term as president, Donald Trump has continuously done both.

To understand how Trump has abused his power against the states, it’s important to understand the power the federal government—and the president, specifically—does have.

For example, the widely varying geographic, demographic, social, and economic circumstances of the states has meant that they need different things from the central government. Thus, the unruly interaction of democratic politics with national government accepts a good deal of horse trading over which states will get various types of federal largesse and regulation, along with a degree of more or less constant disagreement between state and federal authorities over policy and resource allocation.

In extreme cases, the federal government may employ coercion against states that are sufficiently out of harmony with national law and policy. If a state government openly violates federal law despite clear orders from the federal judiciary—as was the case of some Southern states during the civil rights conflicts of the 20th century—the national government may use appropriate measures, including force, to compel compliance with the law. This is not the current circumstance.

Critically, the federal government has to enforce such measures itself rather than commandeering the states to do so. Congress lacks “the power to issue orders directly to the States.” It cannot compel states to issue regulations. It cannot command state officers to participate in or enforce federal laws under what is known as the anti-commandeering doctrine.

While Congress can condition a state’s receipt of federal funds on compliance with specified conditions, there are limitations to this power. Congress’ conditions to states must be clear and unambiguous and must have some relationship to the purposes of the federal grants in question. The conditions cannot be imposed without a state’s knowing and voluntary consent. This means that Congress may not set conditions on dispersal of federal funds that effectively offer the state no realistic choice except compliance.

While Congress has some authority to induce states to participate in federal initiatives, the president acting on his own authority has no such power. To be sure, the president and the executive branch are charged with lawfully implementing congressional directives about the dispersal of appropriated funds. But the president cannot discriminate between states in dispersing federal funds by imposing his own rules, policy stipulations, or personal preferences, particularly if they contradict or are unrelated to congressional funding directives. Moreover, the post–Civil War 14th Amendment made explicit that the individual inhabitants of states are entitled to equal treatment under national law, which means that people living in different states cannot be treated differently simply because one lives in a state politically aligned with the president and another does not.

Trump has flagrantly violated these principles on multiple occasions during his second term. The first violation began on his first day back in office when he issued an executive order commanding that “sanctuary jurisdictions,” meaning states, counties, or municipalities that did not order their law-enforcement authorities to cooperate fully with Trump’s immigration-enforcement actions, “do not receive access to Federal funds.” The initial executive order was followed by two others with the same thrust. These orders are not based on any congressional enactment conditioning federal funding on state or local cooperation with federal immigration efforts. Trump renewed the threat to all federal funding in a statement in January 2026.

Following Trump’s executive orders, various elements of the executive branch began to withhold funding to state, regional, and local governments deemed insufficiently compliant with, or openly resistant to, Trump’s immigration program. A number of cities and states that suffered funding cuts sued. At least one court has ruled the cuts illegal. Multiple cases are pending. It is relevant to any article of impeachment premised wholly or in part on coercion of the states over immigration policy that Trump tried essentially the same tactic in his first administration and was blocked by the federal courts. In short, the courts previously ruled that Trump impinged on the sovereignty of the states and ignored Congress’ power of the purse, but he came right back and did it again. This sort of repeat-offender behavior elevates what might otherwise be considered a simple policy or legal dispute into an impeachable offense.

As troublesome as Trump’s extortion of state cooperation with his immigration efforts may be, it is at least connected to an articulable policy objective, however controversial. Two other types of denial of federal funds, grants, or programs are even more concerning, and even more compelling as grounds for impeachment.

First, the Trump administration has actively discriminated against “blue” states by systemically withholding federal funding, grants, and programmatic assistance. The discrimination is self-evident from the available data. A review of presidential disaster declarations entitling states and localities to federal aid revealed that in Trump’s first 14 months in office, he approved a mere 23 percent of applications from states with a Democratic governor and two Democratic senators, while approving 89 percent of requests from states with a Republican governor and two Republican senators. Moreover, approvals of disaster declarations in Democratic states took twice as long as those to Republican states (80 days vs. 40 days). No pattern remotely similar has ever been observed for past presidents.

Moreover, one need not rely on inferences from data. In the fall of 2025, Russell Vought, head of the Office of Management and Budget, announced cancellation of “nearly $8 billion” in grants for clean-energy programs authorized by Congress during the Biden administration—what Vought called the “Green New Scam.” The first indication that these cancellations, in addition to being open violations of Congress’ power of the purse, were based primarily on politics rather than climate policy was that he listed the states in which grants were canceled—and they included no states dominated by Republicans and instead included 16 of the 19 states that had voted for Kamala Harris in the 2024 election. Multiple states, a coalition including energy and environmental organizations and the city of St. Paul, Minnesota, a group of University of California researchers, and others sued the Trump administration over the cancellations. In pleadings filed in the researchers’ case, the U.S. Department of Energy formally stipulated that none of the 284 grants terminated in October 2025 were terminated “based on any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction or performance-based factor.” The stipulation admitted that, “with one exception, the 284 terminated grants had a recipient location and/or at least one place of performance in a state that awarded its electoral votes to Kamala Harris in the 2024 election and has two Democratic-caucusing senators.” The stipulation concluded by confessing:

 DOE accepts that the inclusion of grants in the October notice tranche was based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient’s state. …DOE accepts that the differential treatment resulting in the October 2025 termination of Blue State grants and the non-termination of non-Blue State grants was not based on a rational connection between the recipient’s location and/or place of performance and DOE’s past or current agency priorities.

As reported by the New York Times, at the same time as the administration was cancelling grants to “blue states,” it “left untouched hundreds of additional energy grants in states that were represented by Republicans and had backed Trump in the last election.” In short, the Trump administration has admitted using payment or withholding of congressionally appropriated funds to punish or retaliate against states and their inhabitants because, and only because, those states support the president’s political opposition.

Second, Trump has gone beyond generic discrimination against states controlled by Democrats and, in at least one case, organized a multipronged attack on a single state because its criminal justice system prosecuted, convicted, and refused to release a Trump backer and election denier. Following the 2020 election, Tina Peters, the clerk and recorder of Mesa County, Colorado, was convicted of multiple felonies for breaching the county election systems in a supposed effort to prove that the election had been rigged and lying about it thereafter. In October 2024, Peters was sentenced to nine years in prison.

In the years since 2020, Peters had become a prominent figure in the election-denialist circles supporting Trump, persisting in unsubstantiated claims that somehow Trump had been cheated out of the election against Joe Biden. When Peters was sentenced, Trump declared himself outraged. In August 2025, he demanded that Colorado release Peters, threatening that if it did not, “I am going to take harsh measures.” On Dec. 11, 2025, Trump issued what he characterized as a pardon of Peters. The president’s pardon power does not extend to state crimes.

At the same time Trump was issuing his counterfeit pardon, he was reportedly fuming behind the scenes. On Dec. 15, 2025, White House special assistant Emily Underwood sent an email to five federal agencies organizing an urgent “brainstorm call” in order to, in her words, “prioritize Colorado for the purposes of ensuring grants and federal support are in line with administration priorities.” The next day, the Departments of Transportation and Energy, which had been invited to the “brainstorm,” canceled hundreds of millions of dollars in federal grants for projects in Colorado.

In addition to the cuts in transportation and energy projects, two days after the “brainstorm” call, the Trump administration ordered that Boulder’s National Center for Atmospheric Research, a world leader in climate and earth systems research, be dismantled, shuttering some programs and moving others out of state. In late December, Trump denied two Colorado disaster relief requests stemming from wildfires and a flood. Also in December, the Department of Agriculture attacked Colorado’s federally supported Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program by imposing new requirements that would have been impossible to meet. On Dec. 30, 2025, Trump used his presidential veto to kill a congressionally authorized water project for the Eastern Plains region of Colorado. If there were any doubt about the connection between all these actions and Trump’s fury over the Peters prosecution, Trump removed them with a New Year’s Eve social media post in which he said, of Colorado Gov. Jared Polis and the Republican district attorney who prosecuted Peters: “I wish them only the worst,” and they should “rot in Hell.”

Trump’s assault on Colorado was, if anything, more constitutionally egregious than his general attacks on other Democratic states. In his actions against other states, Trump and his minions were simply giving rein to general political animus or, in some cases, selectively applying his peculiar policy fixations, such as his hatred of clean energy. In Colorado, Trump employed the might of the federal government to coerce a state into granting undeserved personal relief to one properly convicted state felon. Worse, the felon in question was a figurehead in Trump’s ongoing effort to destroy confidence in the nation’s electoral system. Worst of all, the pressure worked: Polis granted Peters clemency in May and she was released in June, after having served less than a quarter of her original sentence. This was as blatant, and impeachable, an abuse of presidential power as can well be imagined.

Multiple courts have entered orders blocking parts of Trump’s funding and program cancellations in states led by Democrats. In particular, in January 2026, a federal judge enjoined the assault on Colorado’s SNAP requirements. The move to dismantle NCAR was enjoined by the same federal court in June 2026; the court determined that the government’s action was procedurally “arbitrary and capricious” and that “retaliation played at least some role.”

However, the question of whether presidential action is impeachable does not turn on the judgments of courts, particularly when the essential ground for an article of impeachment is the president’s active subversion of the basic constitutional design. It is absolutely plain that the president may not consciously discriminate against a state government or the residents of a state based purely on the partisan political alignment of the state’s residents or its government. Nor can a president enlist the power of the federal government to coerce a state’s justice system into granting special treatment to a personal favorite of the president, particularly if that favorite’s crime was committed in aid of the president’s own attack on the nation’s electoral system.

Considered together, Trump’s partisan attacks on Democratic states and their residents amount to an abuse of presidential power sufficiently egregious and disruptive of constitutional order to merit impeachment.
news.summary: The Trump administration has actively discriminated against “blue” states by systemically withholding money. That's not the worst part.

news.title: Everything you need to know about the chaotic multi-billion-dollar battle for Senate majority
news.text:
Control of the Senate has unexpectedly become a closely contested battle with less than two months remaining until Election Day, despite earlier expectations that Republicans would comfortably maintain their majority for the final two full years of President Donald Trump’s term.

President Donald Trump’s declining approval ratings and widespread voter dissatisfaction with the economy have created a tough political landscape for Republicans, allowing Democrats to compete in once-unreachable states. However, several races Democrats previously counted on winning have also grown increasingly complicated.

Total campaign spending across these midterm Senate contests is projected to surpass $3.4 billion. The overall stakes remain significant for Trump’s broader agenda and his ability to fill administration vacancies and open court seats, since the Senate can confirm or block presidential nominees.

Republican officials maintain it is unlikely every key race will break in favor of Democrats, though they concede the current conditions are difficult. Senate Majority Leader John Thune told South Dakota’s KELOLAND News last week that he does "worry" about losing the chamber.

"I’m a realist," Thune said. "I don’t ever try and sugarcoat things. I think it’s a competitive environment right now."

Democrats need a net gain of four seats to capture the Senate majority. Their original roadmap relied on holding Michigan, Georgia and New Hampshire while retaking Republican-held seats in Alaska, Maine, North Carolina and Ohio. However, the map's dynamics have evolved.

"We now have multiple paths for the majority," Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said last month. "We found new states — Iowa, Texas — which people a year ago weren’t even paying attention to." Yet some states where Democrats felt most optimistic at the start of the election cycle, including Michigan and Maine, have grown considerably more complicated.

In Michigan, an open seat this fall offers a battleground where no GOP contender has won a Senate election since 1994. Still, Democrats are struggling to unite behind nominee Abdul El-Sayed. The progressive favorite narrowly edged moderate U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens in the August primary, leaving raw feelings after a punishing race in which almost $70 million was poured into ads against El-Sayed.

Republicans see an improved prospect for Mike Rogers, who fell short in the 2024 Senate race by fewer than 20,000 votes, to defeat El-Sayed. The Senate Leadership Fund — Senate Republicans’ spending PAC — injected an additional $6 million into its Michigan advertising campaign following El-Sayed’s primary victory, pushing their total investment to $51 million, the third-highest total nationally. 

Meanwhile, Democrats previously identified a strong opportunity to finally unseat five-term Republican Sen. Susan Collins in Maine, where Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris captured more votes than Trump in 2024.

Progressive Graham Platner won the nomination handily in June, but exited the contest the following month over a sexual assault allegation that he denies. In late July, Democratic delegates picked Troy Jackson, a lesser-known former state legislative leader, as his replacement.

Jackson has consequently been forced to play catch-up. Collins and her aligned super PACs have spent nearly $80 million to date, according to ad-tracking firm AdImpact, whereas Jackson and Democratic-aligned groups have spent and reserved close to $45 million since he stepped into the nomination.

Democrats increasingly view real electoral opportunities in several Republican-led states, including Iowa, Alaska, Ohio, and Texas—a long-elusive target for the party.

In Texas, Democrat James Talarico is contesting state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who ousted four-term incumbent Republican Sen. John Cornyn during the GOP primary. Senate GOP leaders had supported Cornyn, believing he was the more formidable candidate for the general election.

Legal and ethical questions have shadowed Paxton for decades, including securities fraud indictments that did not result in a conviction.

Talarico and allied organizations have invested nearly $30 million in advertising since the May runoff, whereas pro-Paxton groups have spent under $3 million. Last week, a political fund associated with Trump injected $10 million into digital and television ads for Paxton, marking the first substantial general election investment by MAGA Inc. this midterm cycle. Senate GOP leaders had urged Trump’s political team to deploy part of the more than $400 million it held last month to help Paxton.

Democrats have also escalated spending across GOP-held battlegrounds in Alaska, Iowa, Ohio, and North Carolina. Meanwhile, Republicans report heightened optimism regarding Michigan and New Hampshire, while committing additional resources to defend seats in Iowa and Alaska.

This broadened map has increased overall projected spending. In June, AdImpact projected $3.4 billion would be spent on Senate race advertising, representing a marked rise from the $2.8 billion forecasted in the fall of 2025.

Democratic prospects have expanded partly because of Trump’s declining job approval, particularly on economic management, which stood at 32% in a July AP-NORC poll — down from 40% in March 2025, shortly after he entered office.

Trump’s commercial policies alongside the conflict in Iran, with corresponding inflated fuel costs, have heightened economic unpredictability for voters under two months before Election Day. "Things still cost too much. And so we’ve got to work on that issue," Republican Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio told The Associated Press. "We understand that and we know that’s real."

Ohio Sen. Jon Husted heard these anxieties directly at a roundtable last month. Husted is attempting to hold off a comeback from former Sen. Sherrod Brown in another crucial contest for both parties.

During a discussion on housing, one participant told Husted that expenses were "skyrocketing" partly due to uncertainty around tariffs.

"Uncertainty is the killer to this economy," said Dean Windham, a real estate developer who previously ran for office as a Republican.

Some Republican Senate candidates have defended Trump’s measures while confronting concerns over economic fallout.

In Michigan, where Trump’s tariffs on Canada have become a central topic, Rogers has supported the president’s strategy while leaving room for disagreement.

"President Trump is right to put America First — and tariffs are necessary, but are not a one-size-fits-all solution," Rogers said in a recent statement.

Even if Democrats retain every seat they currently control, securing a majority would require flipping at least two seats in states Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

Republicans are betting these foundational advantages will matter more as Election Day nears — particularly as Trump and the party focus on rallying the voters who helped return him to the White House.

Last week, Trump informed reporters he will "be making a lot of stops" in the final 30 days before the election.

Next week, Republicans are holding a midterm convention in Texas, where Trump is scheduled to speak and prominent Senate candidates including Rogers and Husted are expected to attend.

However, Republicans acknowledge they have work to do.

"Politics is local," noted Republican Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota. He pointed to Trump’s decision on importing beef, which he said made farmers and ranchers "feel just like the administration pulled the rug right off from underneath" them.

"They’re hurt," said Rounds. "They feel like they’ve been let down."
news.summary: Democrats have found themselves competing in states that once seemed beyond their reach

news.title: Exclusive poll: GOP's gains among Latinos fade in House battlegrounds
news.text:
Coming out of the 2024 election, Republicans hoped Trump's near-parity with Democrats among Latinos in 2024 would harden into a lasting political realignment favoring the GOP. Instead, this poll and surveys earlier this year suggest that the nation's fastest-growing swing electorate is moving left, as anger at high prices and Trump's immigration policies appear to be giving Democrats an opening.

By the numbers: Democrats are gaining ground with Latino voters across a survey of 17 competitive House districts, opening a 58%-35% lead on the generic congressional ballot, according to the Hart Research for TelevisaUnivision poll.

That 23-point margin is double the 11-point edge Kamala Harris held over Trump in the same sample's self-reported 2024 vote.Among Spanish-language media consumers, Democrats lead the 2026 generic ballot by 14 points, compared with a 1-point Trump edge in the group's self-reported 2024 vote.

Zoom in: In three Texas congressional districts — one on the Mexico border, another in suburban Fort Worth and another in the Austin-San Antonio corridor — Latino voters went from a self-reported 44-44 split in the 2024 presidential race to 56-36 in Democrats' favor today.

In Florida, Latino voters in two swing districts have gone from Trump +1 to Democrat +13 in the same period, the poll found.

The intrigue: 11% of Latino voters who say they backed Trump in 2024 now support Democratic congressional candidates.

State of play: Overall, Trump is deeply underwater with Latino voters in these battleground districts.

63% disapprove of his overall job performance, compared with 36% who approve.65% disapprove of Trump's handling of prices and the cost of living, while 62% disapprove of his administration's immigration enforcement and deportations.That marks a striking reversal from 2024, when Trump's gains with Latino voters helped produce the most racially diverse Republican presidential coalition in decades.

What they're saying: "Latino voters aren't locked into one party. They're paying close attention and making decisions based on who shows up for them, and how they're showing up," TelevisaUnivision Senior Vice President Kate Coleman tells Axios.

Aileen Cardona-Arroyo, a partner at Hart Research, tells Axios the survey showed Spanish language media is critical for engaging Latino voters in 2026 competitive congressional races. 

Trump's immigration crackdown appears to have run into a wall with these voters — without producing a wholesale rejection of strict border enforcement.

ICE has a 64% unfavorable rating, including 65% among Latino independents.

Zoom out: The economy still outranks immigration as Latino voters' top concern, the survey indicates.

Democrats hold an advantage on the issue that helped Trump make gains among Latinos two years ago: 62% trust Democrats in Congress more to lower prices, versus 36% who trust Republicans more. 

Methodology: The 2026 Latino Battleground survey included 1,500 Latino registered voters in 17 battleground congressional districts and was conducted Aug. 6-17, 2026, by Hart Research for TelevisaUnivision.

The margin of sampling error is ±2,5 percentage points for Latino adults at the 95% confidence level.

news.title: At the Races: Don’t take it for Granite
news.text:
Welcome to a special edition of At the Races! Throughout the 2026 primary season, watch for these updates from the CQ Roll Call campaign team on what you need to know for Election Day. Know someone who’d like to get this newsletter? They can subscribe here.

By Mary Ellen McIntire, Andrew Menezes and Daniela Altimari

Labor Day typically marks the kickoff of the general election campaign, but there are still a few primaries to settle first. 

One of those states is battleground New Hampshire, where Democrats on Tuesday will wrap up a bitter battle to pick their nominee for the 1st District seat Rep. Chris Pappas is vacating to run for Senate. 

Polls have shown a close Democratic primary race between Marine Corps veteran Maura Sullivan and former Portsmouth City Councilor Stefany Shaheen, the daughter of retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. Several other candidates will appear on the ballot, including Hampton Select Board Chairwoman Carleigh Beriont, who is trying to stake out the progressive lane. Former Pentagon lawyer Christian Urrutia, who was also running as a progressive, dropped his campaign over the weekend and endorsed Shaheen. His name remains on the ballot. 

The race between Sullivan and Shaheen has grown increasingly negative. Shaheen has accused Sullivan’s campaign of being funded by AIPAC donors, while Sullivan’s team has gone after Shaheen’s “fancy last name.” With such a late primary, the winner will have to quickly unite the party heading into the fall election. 

Republicans are hoping to wage a more competitive campaign in the 1st District this year without an incumbent on the ballot. Kamala Harris carried the district, which covers eastern New Hampshire, by 2 points in 2024, and strong Republican performances in the state’s gubernatorial and Senate races could help boost the party’s 1st District nominee. Businessman Anthony DiLorenzo, who has largely self-funded his campaign, has President Donald Trump’s endorsement and is backed by the NRCC. 

But first he has to get past businesswoman Hollie Noveletsky, who ran for the seat two years ago, and state Rep. Brian Cole. Two other candidates who’ve ended their campaigns and endorsed DiLorenzo will also be on the ballot. 

Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales rates the general election for the 1st District as Lean Democratic. 

In the 2nd District primary, Democratic incumbent Maggie Goodlander is being challenged from the left by state Rep. Paige Beauchemin. On the Republican side, activist Lily Tang Williams faces three opponents as she makes her third straight bid for the seat. In 2024, she lost to Goodlander by 6 points. 

Inside Elections rates the race Likely Democratic. 

Battleground Senate race

New Hampshire’s Senate race could be among the most competitive this year. Inside Elections moved it into the Toss-up category last week, and recent polls have shown the November election within the margin of error.

Pappas is looking for a decisive win in the Democratic primary over biochemist Karishma Manzur, whose progressive campaign appears to have picked up momentum in the contest’s closing stages. Pappas campaigned this weekend with both Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly.

On the GOP side, former Sen. John E. Sununu has Trump’s support and is favored to claim the nomination 18 years after he lost reelection to Jeanne Shaheen. Like Pappas, he too has to get past a primary opponent Tuesday. Former Massachusetts Sen. Scott P. Brown is making his second Senate run from the Granite State.

New Hampshire hasn’t elected a Republican to the Senate since 2010, but the party has signaled some optimism about the race in a year in which Democrats have more offensive opportunities across the country. 

Rhode Island votes Wednesday

The Ocean State is holding its primaries Wednesday, a day later than usual to ease matters for election workers post-Labor Day.

Democrats are expected to dominate congressional races in Rhode Island this fall, including Sen. Jack Reed, who faces two primary opponents Tuesday. Democratic Reps. Gabe Amo and Seth Magaziner are unopposed in the primaries for their deep-blue seats. 

Perhaps a more interesting contest is the Democratic primary for governor. Polls have shown Gov. Dan McKee trailing challenger Helena Buonanno Foulkes, a former CVS executive who narrowly lost to him in the 2022 primary. 

Foulkes has a couple of notable connections to Congress. Her maternal grandfather, Thomas J. Dodd, and uncle Christopher J. Dodd represented Connecticut in the Senate and House. And her late mother was a college roommate of former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who campaigned for Foulkes in Providence late last month.

news.title: Vulnerable Republicans face a Trump-sized dilemma: Keep your distance or lean in
news.text:
As the midterm elections approach, vulnerable Republicans are confronting an increasingly unavoidable question: Should they distance themselves from the president, or lean in to him?

Donald Trump remains a powerful force for turning out the voters that Republicans need in November. But his low approval ratings and growing political liabilities have also given vulnerable GOP lawmakers reason to stay away, particularly in districts where they need to win over voters who are less firmly aligned with the president.

The question is particularly urgent this week, as Trump prepares to headline the GOP’s first-ever midterm convention in Dallas and Republicans weigh whether they should attend.

For Republican Rep. Mike Lawler, who’s running for his third term in a suburban district outside of New York City, the answer seems obvious: Embrace Trump. 

Even though Kamala Harris carried his district in 2024, Lawler is speaking at the GOP convention. And back in May, the embattled Republican held a joint rally with Trump in Suffern, New York. In short, Lawler doesn’t seem to have any concerns about hitching his wagon to the president.

“My district obviously is what it is, but for me, it's very simple,” Lawler told MS NOW. “I've always been very clear. If I disagree, I say it.”

“People in my district understand that I'm delivering for them,” Lawler continued. “They may not always agree with me. They may not like everything that I say. But the fact is, I have put our district front and center in making decisions in this country in a way that really was never the case.”

In Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District — a swing-seat suburb outside of Des Moines — Rep. Zach Nunn is doing a similar calculus.

“He’s had two rallies in our district,” Nunn said of Trump, “and I attended.”

Asked if he feels the president “helps” his re-election cause, Nunn disputed the premise of the question — “with respect, that is not the right question to be asking” — before clarifying that, “on the issues that are important to Iowans, I'm 100 percent with the president.” 

“On the issues where he doesn't help Iowans,” Nunn continued, “I'm the first to stand up and tell the president this is not working out.”

Across the country, even as his approval ratings fall as gas prices rise, vulnerable Republicans have similarly chosen to appear alongside Trump when he has come to their battleground districts.

That list includes Lawler, Nunn, Rep. Juan Ciscomani in Arizona’s 1st district, Rep. Tom Barrett in Michigan’s 7th district, Ryan Mackenzie in Pennsylvania’s 7th district and Rep. Derrick Van Orden in Wisconsin’s 3rd district — all of whom are running in races rated “toss up” by Cook Political Report.

Some, like Lawler and Nunn, are downplaying the impact Trump will have in their districts. They contend voters will make up their minds independent of Trump. But where other lawmakers in swing districts might historically distance themselves from an unpopular president, many Republicans this year suggested they see Trump as an asset. 

Van Orden, a two-term congressman representing an R+3 district, said it was “not a question at all” of whether he’d appear with Trump in his Badger State district. He even noted that Trump seems to have more pull in the district: Trump won the area by 7.4 points in 2024 while Van Orden secured reelection by just 2.8%.

“If you want to talk politically, he won my district three times in a row,” Van Orden said of Trump. “I underperformed him three times in a row.”

Wisconsin Public Radio recently noted that Van Orden and his fellow Wisconsin Republican Bryan Steil are standing by Trump, even as the president’s popularity fades. But Van Orden, who was on Capitol grounds as a protester on Jan. 6, would have a difficult time separating his brand from the president.

While Van Orden suggested aligning himself with Trump was good politics, he said the politics was “secondary.”

“President Trump literally got shot in the head for America,” Van Orden told MS NOW. “He got shot in the head for America. He could be retired on some super yacht in the Caribbean doing whatever he wanted, but he stood up to fight for our country.”

“I'm not backing away from that guy,” Van Orden continued.

For Democrats, that decision is welcome news.

With Trump’s approval rating underwater — 39.7%, according to Real Clear Politics — Democrats have no problem watching their top opponents run with the president.

“Donald Trump completely is not in contact with the average voter when it comes to affordability — in fact, he keeps dismissing it in a pretty offensive way, I think, for most voters,” Rep. Mark Pocan, D-Wis., a vice-chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, told MS NOW.

“Everything we’ve seen, especially with independents, it’s a bad message for them,” Pocan said. “So the more they’re connected to that, it just reminds people that they’re doing nothing about what they and their family cares about — and that’s good for us.”

Pocan’s argument is essentially that Republicans have little choice but to stick with Trump, even if doing so creates political problems of its own.

“They just can’t walk away,” Pocan said, “even though all the facts around them are that he’s probably not the person you want to campaign with side-by-side.”

Other Democrats were even blunter.

“It’s the worst catch-22 for them,” a Democratic operative working on House races said of the GOP decision to campaign with Trump. “Great for us though!”

Still, whether Republicans campaign with Trump exists on a spectrum. Appearing alongside the president does not necessarily mean making him the centerpiece of a campaign. Most GOP ads focus on issues of affordability and cost of living.

Of course, not every Republican is embracing the president with open arms. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania — one of the Republicans representing a district Harris won in 2024 — has broken with Trump several times throughout his career. But Fitzpatrick said the answer was to make the race about your district, rather than tearing your hair out about how much distance to put between yourself and Trump.

“I think people overcomplicate this,” Fitzpatrick told MS NOW. “We all represent a constituency and we have to be loyal to them.”

“Most districts, particularly mine, they don't want you to be the permanent lapdog nor the permanent critic of any administration,” Fitzpatrick continued. “They want you to call balls and strikes based on what's good for the people back home.”

“We don't need to get into pro-Trump, anti-Trump, pro-Biden, anti-Biden,” Fitzpatrick added. “I think people get too hung up on people or presidents when it’s about a district — and no district is 100% for or 100% against anybody.”

While Fitzpatrick doesn’t see Trump as a defining issue, the White House and Republican Party are making it increasingly difficult for GOP candidates to avoid him.

The party’s unprecedented midterm convention in Dallas this week will put the president front and center, and remind voters how he looms over all politics.

The White House is also thrusting Trump to the forefront with new ads — from a super PAC aligned with the president — that feature Trump prominently.

Vice President JD Vance sought to give GOP lawmakers some space from the administration if they thought that would benefit them — “we don't need a congressman in a tight race to be there in all cases” he said of the convention — but vulnerable Republicans are making different calculations about whether their time is better spent alongside Trump or back home with voters.

Trump himself has made it clear that he intends to play a central role in the midterm campaign, arguing that Republicans should run on his record.

But if national figures are going to swing elections, Lawler thinks that affects more than just members of his party.

“Everybody focuses directly on Trump,” Lawler said. But, “in a blue state like New York where Democrats control everything,” Lawler said New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Sen. Chuck Schumer would also affect votes.

Of course, not everyone thinks the decision of whether to distance yourself from Trump or to embrace him is all that consequential.

As one vulnerable Republican put it, Trump is inescapable either way.

“He’s the fucking president,” the lawmaker said. “Get over it.”

news.title: New Hampshire votes today in a Senate race Democrats no longer feel is safe
news.text:
Democrats spent this cycle expanding the Senate map deep into Republican territory — Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Alaska. Now, eight weeks from Election Day, the surprise is running the other direction, too: New Hampshire, which hasn't had a close Senate race since Donald Trump was first elected president, is suddenly on the map.

Tuesday's primaries are expected to set the matchup. Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas is fending off a challenge from progressive Karishma Manzur for the seat being vacated by Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. On the Republican side, two former senators — John Sununu and Scott Brown — are competing for the nomination. Pappas and Sununu are heavily favored, and both have spent the primary running as though the general election has already begun.

National Democrats hit the snooze button on New Hampshire for a year. They are not anymore. 

The reasons why are not complicated. 

“It's because of Sununu,” a Democratic operative told MS NOW, granted anonymity to speak about internal dynamics on the Pappas campaign. ”It's the only place where they got a recruit, right?”

In Sununu, Washington Republicans landed the candidate they wanted — a former senator, the brother of a recent popular former governor and the son of another former governor, with a family name that has been on ballots here for decades. National Republican groups have spent accordingly: Outside GOP ad spending in the race has topped $30 million, according to ad trackers. And incumbent Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte is up for re-election this year in a race she’s widely expected to win — with the potential for coattails for GOP candidates down the ticket.

New Hampshire Republicans want to make the midterm election about state and local issues. Democrats want a referendum on Trump. The state's famously independent voters will decide which argument lands.

Sununu has largely avoided the national press, instead opting for a hyperlocal campaign. He has not hesitated, however, to welcome the flood of outside money not arriving on his behalf — a cash influx that has alarmed Pappas’ campaign.

Pappas, a four-term congressman, has outraised his likely general election opponent in direct contributions. But that advantage is dwarfed by the millions flowing to Sununu from the Senate Leadership Fund, the National Republican Senatorial Committee, AFP Action, One Nation and Republican megadonor Elon Musk.

“We're taking nothing for granted, this is a purple state,” Pappas told MS NOW. “We've got a path to victory. But it's going to be a tough race.”

His answer has been to embrace national Democrats rather than keep them at arm’s length. Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., both potential 2028 contenders testing out their messages in the early-primary state, campaigned across New Hampshire for Democrats over Labor Day weekend. Pappas also touted an endorsement from former Vice President Kamala Harris, even as other Democratic candidates — Iowa’s Rob Sand and Josh Turek, Alaska’s Mary Peltola — have shied away from her support.

"I think her voice is going to continue to be important for the Democratic Party moving forward," Pappas said in an interview. "We need all the voices in the tent, and the only way we're going to win elections in purple states like this is to bring together moderates and progressives and independents and pro-democracy Republicans and people that are opposed to Trump's policies."

First, though, he has to get past Manzur, who has attacked him for accepting donations from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee — a line of criticism he has dodged on the debate stage and in interviews.

“It’s not just about AIPAC. We're trying to get money out of politics,” Manzur told MS NOW. “We want our lawmakers to answer to the people, not to their donors, not to special interests.”

Manzur has repeatedly refused to say she would back Pappas in the general election if he is the nominee.

Democrats in the state are not especially worried about the primary. “I think it's just the cycle for these things to be coming up,” the Democratic operative in New Hampshire told MS NOW, downplaying the possibility of a Manzur upset. Candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America have won elsewhere, the operative acknowledged, but New Hampshire's independent streak makes for harder ground: "It's just a less hospitable environment for it, frankly."

In the Republican primary, Brown has criticized Sununu as missing in action. 

“At least I'm showing up,” Brown told MS NOW at a Labor Day parade in Milford. “I'm not avoiding debates, and I'm answering every and all questions. And he's not.”

Sununu, who once called Trump a “loser,” has barely mentioned the president’s endorsement — a distance Brown has seized on. 

“He's embarrassed by it,” Brown said. “What did he give up to get that endorsement? I call balls and strikes. That's why I didn't get it. … I don't want Canada to be the 51st state. I want this war in Iran to end.” 

Those attacks have not moved much. Sununu has maintained a healthy double-digit lead over Brown in polls. But the general election is likely to be fought on different ground between two candidates who have been fixtures in New Hampshire politics for years and who generate little of the noise that draws national attention.

That is part of why the race went unnoticed for so long, said Neil Levesque, executive director of the New Hampshire Institute of Politics at Saint Anselm College.

“They're not exactly candidates that do these sort of outrageous things or say these outrageous things,” he said. “They're very strong and steady — no drama — and so that's probably what's attracted less attention. But one seat in the Senate is one seat. They're all the same value.”

Levesque expects Social Security, tariffs, corruption and the Iran war to dominate the fall — sentiments echoed by voters. “Trump has always won on the economy. He can't anymore because of the high prices, the war, etc.,” he said. “People who are concerned about the economy are the people I would watch.”

Mike Dennehy, a longtime New Hampshire Republican operative, is bullish on Sununu, arguing that his name recognition combined with Ayotte’s popularity is “a one-two punch” the state has rarely seen. 

“Sununu's strength is that he is a fantastic campaigner. He knows New Hampshire, he knows the people, and he's always been able to connect with voters about their concerns, voters can see him as a U.S. senator because he was a U.S. senator,” Dennehy said. “If he loses, it would just be simply because of a national wave against the Republican Party.”

Voters, meanwhile, described an economy they cannot make sense of and a politics they are tired of.

Joanne Palys, 65, said the economy “totally sucks” and she hopes Pappas wins the general election.

“I'm very scared about this election because I've been very depressed,” Palys told MS NOW. She said her top issue is to “get rid of Trump” and his supporters in government.

Mike Turner, a self-described “Reagan conservative,” said inflation is “out of control” and “unbearable,” and criticized Trump’s trade war against Canada. “Tariffs are evil,” he said. But he plans to vote for Sununu and said he would stick with the Republican ticket regardless of Tuesday's result.

Jaime Beckford, a 34-year-old healthcare worker, said she is “really disappointed in just everything” and not sure which party's primary ballot she’ll choose on Tuesday.

“I have a hard time just committing to one or the other,” she said.

She will decide on Tuesday. Then both parties will spend the next eight weeks counting on her to decide again.
